Back to Healio Save Share LinkedIn Facebook X (Twitter) Bluesky Threads Email Copy Link Key takeaways: The addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to first-line R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% for patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said. “The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. Perspective Back to Top Krish Patel, MD Krish Patel, MD For more than 2 decades, R-CHOP has been the global standard of care for newly diagnosed patients with DLBCL, leading to cure in about 60% of patients. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. Krish Patel, MD SCRI Oncology Partners Sarah Cannon Research Institute Disclosures: Patel reports research funding to his institution from, consulting/advisory roles with or speakers bureau roles with AbbVie, AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Genentech, Genmab, Janssen, Kite Pharma, Merck, Pfizer, Sanofi and other companies. Perspective Back to Top Tycel Phillips, MD Tycel Phillips, MD Improving response and curability remains paramount for management of patients with first-line DLBCL, despite improvement of salvage options. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Tycel Phillips, MD City of Hope Disclosures: Phillips reports research support from, advisory board roles with or scientific board roles with AbbVie, Adaptive, ADC Therapeutics, AstraZeneca, BeOne Medicines, Bristol Myers Squibb, Caribou, Eli Lilly & Co., Epizyme, Genentech, Genmab, Gilead Sciences, Incyte, Janssen/Johnson & Johnson, Kite Pharma, Legend Biotech, Merck, Pfizer, Pharmacyclics, Seagen and Sobi. The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said. “The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? Perspective Back to Top Tycel Phillips, MD Tycel Phillips, MD Improving response and curability remains paramount for management of patients with first-line DLBCL, despite improvement of salvage options. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Key takeaways:
The addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to first-line R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% for patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The regimen could become a standard in this setting.

The regimen could become a standard in this setting.
CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial.
Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD
Krish Patel, MD;
Tycel Phillips, MD
The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed.
diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago.
The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting.
Georg Lenz
“I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.”
Georg Lenz, MD
An unmet need
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases.
R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades.
However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease.
“We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said.
Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant.
The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL.
Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas.
The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL.
All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment.
Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles.
PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints.
‘Good chance’ for cure
Median follow-up reached 35.2 months.
The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed.
The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin.
Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%).
“Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.”
Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%).
An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival.
“We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said.
‘Manageable’ toxicities
The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events.
Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%).
More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%).
Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles.
“The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.”
Evolving treatment landscape
The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment.
The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting.
The New England Journal of Medicine
Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment.
The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL.
epcoritamab
The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said.
“The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out.
“Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.”

The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Skip to content Suggested Topics: Home Best in Biotech Eight oncology deals in 2026 spotlight where industry leaders are betting big Photo credits: Cytonn Photography (Unsplash) Newsletter Signup - Under Article / In Page " * " indicates required fields Biotech partnerships play a critical role in driving innovation through the sharing of knowledge, expertise, and resources, and are particularly important in bridging the gap between early-stage research and commercial development. As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. In this article, we look at eight of the biggest oncology deals that have been made so far in 2026. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China. The radiopharmaceutical revolution: From diagnosis to treatment, oncology and beyond Eight biotech companies spearheading the antibody drug conjugate new wave The financial terms of the deal included a $350 million upfront payment for Innovent, with the company also eligible to receive up to approximately $8.5 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments. AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer. Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S. Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership. Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%. VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index. The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales. Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials. Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales. This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die. These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise. Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer. Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization. Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement. As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. In this article, we look at eight of the biggest oncology deals that have been made so far in 2026. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China. AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer. Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S. Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership. Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%. VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index. The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales. Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials. Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales. This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die. These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise. Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer. Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization. Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement. As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership. Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%. Industry News WuXi Biologics gets South Korean GMP certification for bispecific antibody The certification enables end-to-end commercial manufacturing across drug substance, fill-finish, and packaging for complex biologics targeting oncology indications. April 24, 2026 2 min read WuXi Biologics, a global contract research, development, and manufacturing organization (CRDMO), announced that three manufacturing facilities in Wuxi, China, have received Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) certification from South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety, enabling commercial manufacturing of a bispecific antibody for biliary tract cancer. The certification covers the company’s Drug Substance Facility 5, Drug Product Facility 2, and Drug Product Packaging Center, supporting integrated capabilities from drug substance manufacturing through fill-finish and packaging. The approval follows a five-day inspection with no critical or major findings. According to the company , the certified facilities are part of its global GMP network and provide end-to-end manufacturing services designed to support commercial-scale production of complex biologics. The integrated setup is intended to streamline supply and improve operational efficiency for biologics programs targeting global markets. WuXi Biologics said the certification strengthens its ability to support customers in South Korea and the broader Asia-Pacific region, particularly for advanced modalities such as bispecific antibodies. The development aligns with the company’s broader strategy to expand its integrated CRDMO model , which combines research, development and manufacturing capabilities to improve speed, flexibility and consistency across biologics programs. The company has reported growing demand for complex modalities, including bispecific and multispecific antibodies, within its pipeline. April 29, 2026 2 min read shutterstock_2461469693 CellProthera, a biotechnology company headquartered in Mulhouse, France, has entered a collaboration with Quintessence Biotech to optimize cell therapy manufacturing processes ahead of clinical trials for ischemic stroke. The partnership will integrate Quintessence Biotech’s flotation-based cell sorting platform into CellProthera’s manufacturing workflow for its CD34+ cell therapy candidate, with the goal of improving cell yield, preserving stem cell phenotype and enhancing product quality, the company said. The technology is designed to simplify cell sorting by eliminating the need for magnetic separation systems and specialized consumables, while enabling integration into existing cell culture environments, according to the announcement. CellProthera said the collaboration supports its broader manufacturing strategy as it prepares for Phase 3 production of its lead therapy for acute myocardial infarction, while exploring expansion into stroke indications that may require higher cell doses. Further testing will focus on adapting the platform to specific process requirements and scaling manufacturing performance. The agreement builds on CellProthera’s ongoing efforts to establish late-stage manufacturing capabilities. In 2025, the company selected CellforCURE by Seqens to support Phase 3 GMP manufacturing of its CD34+ therapy, including technology transfer and clinical batch production for a planned late-stage trial.
